post.label: Postcolonial history / critique
post.description: Questions imperial knowledge, Eurocentric universals, and the assumption that all societies follow Europe’s historical path.
post.representative_figures_and_works: Edward Said, Orientalism (1978); Gayatri Spivak (1988); Dipesh Chakrabarty, Provincializing Europe (2000). Gyan Prakash: “Writing Post-Orientalist Histories of the Third World” (1990); Stuart Hall: “When Was ‘the Post-colonial’?” (1996); Paul Gilroy: The Black Atlantic (1993).

representative_people.context: Studies imperial authority through texts and institutions, combining discourse analysis with hegemony and attention to particular writers.
representative_people.works: Orientalism (1978)

representative_people.context: Questions intellectual representation through colonialism, labor and gender; uses deconstruction critically.
representative_people.works: “Can the Subaltern Speak?” (1988); A Critique of Postcolonial Reason (1999)

representative_people.context: Tests European social-science categories against South Asian political histories while retaining their critical uses.
representative_people.works: Provincializing Europe (2000); edition with a new preface responding to critics (2007); “In Defense of Provincializing Europe” (2008)

representative_people.context: Develops colonial historical difference through an explicit disagreement with Anderson.
representative_people.works: Nationalist Thought and the Colonial World (1986); The Nation and Its Fragments (1993)

representative_people.context: Examines ambivalence, mimicry and hybrid cultural production; these concepts are debated interpretations.
representative_people.works: The Location of Culture (1994)

representative_people.context: Criticizes homogenizing accounts of women and develops historically situated feminist solidarity.
representative_people.works: “Under Western Eyes” (1984; revised 1991)

representative_people.context: Reworks Foucault through colonial archives, race and sexuality (1995); treats 'colonizer/colonized' as 'a historically shifting pair of social categories that needs to be explained' (2002, p. 13, as quoted by Ottevaere); asks scholars to move 'from archive-as-source to archive-as-subject' (2002). Gouda: homage to her work 'has become de rigueur' in postcolonial studies (2009).
representative_people.works: Race and the Education of Desire (1995); 'Colonial Archives and the Arts of Governance' (2002); Carnal Knowledge and Imperial Power (2002)

representative_people.context: Historical anthropology examines the colonial production of authoritative knowledge in British India.
representative_people.works: Colonialism and Its Forms of Knowledge (1996)

representative_people.context: His criticism of idealized and denigrating images of India supplies a specific resource for Guha’s environmental argument. Original article remains to be distinguished from its documented reception.
representative_people.works: “Orientalist Constructions of India” (1986), especially442, through Guha (1989)

representative_people.context: Historian whose essays set out postcolonial historiography from Indian historiography and read Subaltern Studies as postcolonial criticism. His Subaltern Studies context remains distinct.
representative_people.works: “Writing Post-Orientalist Histories of the Third World” (1990); “Subaltern Studies as Postcolonial Criticism” (1994)

representative_people.context: Cultural theorist whose essays on diasporic identity and on the category of the “post-colonial” are standard resources in postcolonial critique. His cultural-studies context remains separate.
representative_people.works: “Cultural Identity and Diaspora” (1990); “When Was ‘the Post-colonial’? Thinking at the Limit” (1996)

representative_people.context: The Black Atlantic criticizes national and racial closure and reads modernity through the Black Atlantic; a standard postcolonial and diaspora text for historians. His Atlantic and diaspora contexts remain.
representative_people.works: The Black Atlantic (1993)

representative_people.context: Coedited Tensions of Empire with Ann Laura Stoler (1997) and coauthored its opening research-agenda chapter. The publisher describes a historical and anthropological inquiry into relations between metropole and colony and changing categories of colonial rule. This contextual inclusion does not identify Cooper as an adherent of every postcolonial theory; his later criticisms require a separate dated claim.
representative_people.works: Tensions of Empire (1997), coedited with Ann Laura Stoler; opening chapter, “Between Metropole and Colony: Rethinking a Research Agenda”

representative_people.context: Metropole and colony in one frame: Birmingham abolitionists, Baptist missionaries and Jamaica, 1830–1867; read as postcolonial history by Woollacott (2006).
representative_people.works: Civilising Subjects (2002)

representative_people.context: Reads the French headscarf ban and the discourse of secularism as civilizational claims about gender equality, in the accounts of her reviewers Laborde and Whitney and her 2018 interview; Laborde finds the normative premises unclear, and O’Grady objects that the later book holds nineteenth-century Europeans to present moral standards. Scott asks how to critique secularism without rejecting it (2018 interview).
representative_people.works: The Politics of the Veil (2007); Sex and Secularism (2017)

representative_people.context: Takes Hegel’s World-history to task as a statist frame that, in Guha’s words as Michael quotes them, reached India as an instrument of the East India Company, and asks historians to learn from literature the historicality of everyday life (2002), as Michael and Chakrabarty read the book; Michael fears the state may be lost “as an object of critique” and finds the argument largely conceptual.
representative_people.works: History at the Limit of World-History (2002)

representative_people.context: 'A critical indictment of Western historiography' and of 'history telling as a professional activity' (Craipain, 2024); 'not all narratives or narrators are created equal'. Silencing the Past unread; wording awaits a library copy.
representative_people.works: Silencing the Past (1995)

post.scope_note: Said, Spivak, and Chakrabarty address different problems; literary critique and historical scholarship interact without becoming the same discipline. Feminist critiques, colonial archival research and theories of ambivalence introduce further disagreements. These selections do not make postcolonial thought synonymous with South Asian history, literary theory or all anti-colonial politics.

strands.focus: Texts acquire authority through institutions and citation; individual writers remain consequential.

strands.title: Representation and intellectual responsibility
strands.focus: Speaking for others and depicting them pose connected political problems.

strands.title: Provincializing historical categories
strands.focus: Critique works through inherited concepts without treating Europe as every society’s model.

strands.title: Colonial nationalism and difference
strands.focus: Bengal supplies the setting for a disputed account of cultural autonomy and political modernity.

strands.title: Mimicry, ambivalence and hybridity

strands.title: Feminist difference and coalition
strands.focus: Neither women’s situations nor feminist scholarship form a single homogeneous subject.

strands.title: Race, sexuality and colonial archives
strands.focus: Empire becomes part of the history of European bourgeois sexuality (1995). Carnal Knowledge and Imperial Power (2002) made 'the intimate' a matter of state and 'colonizer/colonized' a shifting pair of categories (p. 13, as quoted by Ottevaere); the same year her 'Colonial Archives and the Arts of Governance' moved 'from archive-as-source to archive-as-subject', the programme now carried by the entry archival_turn.
strands.works: Race and the Education of Desire (1995); Carnal Knowledge and Imperial Power (2002); 'Colonial Archives and the Arts of Governance' (2002)

strands.title: Critiquing the romanticized East
strands.focus: Guha applies Inden’s critique of hostile and admiring Orientalist images to environmental appropriations of Asian traditions. This documents a particular reception, without making those traditions homogeneous or certifying Inden’s whole argument.
strands.works: Inden (1986), quoted and discussed by Guha (1989),77–78/note9

strands.title: Metropole and colony in a shared research agenda
strands.focus: Cooper and Stoler’s 1997 edited collection supplies a contextual reading on connections between imperial centres and colonial settings and the historical formation of categories of rule. This is the publisher’s description and contents, not a passage-level check or a claim that one programme defines postcolonial history.
strands.works: Tensions of Empire (1997), especially the opening chapter credited to Stoler and Cooper

global.label: World / global / connected history
global.description: Moves across national containers through comparison, interaction, circulation, and connections. These approaches differ; global scale need not imply one theory of globalization.
global.representative_figures_and_works: William McNeill (1963); Eric Wolf (1982); Sanjay Subrahmanyam (1997); Kenneth Pomeranz (2000).

representative_people.context: World synthesis and an explicit account of historical interpretation; source criticism and better-fitting accounts remain valuable within his ecumenical program.
representative_people.works: The Rise of the West (1963); “Mythistory, or Truth, Myth, History, and Historians” (1986)

representative_people.context: Historical anthropology connects peoples usually separated from accounts of European expansion; the recorded source remains a publisher/retrospective check.
representative_people.works: Europe and the People Without History (1982)

representative_people.context: Reconstructs circulation of people, ideas and goods across local and supraregional settings, criticizing national/area boxes without erasing differences.
representative_people.works: “Connected Histories: Notes towards a Reconfiguration of Early Modern Eurasia” (1997), selected primary pages

representative_people.context: Combines regional comparisons with coal location, overseas resources and colonial coercion; no single factor or uniform Eurasian path suffices.
representative_people.works: The Great Divergence (2000); “Histories for a Less National Age” (AHA presidential address, 2014)

representative_people.context: Questions Eurocentric geographical and historical categories within an interregional history. His vocabulary and civilizational rankings remain open to criticism.

spatialhistory.label: Spatial history / Historical geography
spatialhistory.date_label: Sauer 1925 · Hoskins 1955 · critical spatial studies and historical GIS by the 1990s
spatialhistory.description: Investigates how places, landscapes, territories and spatial relationships are made and transformed through time. Reconstructing past geographies, interpreting maps and colonial naming, tracing contested place identities, and linking historical records through GIS are different practices within this broad field.
spatialhistory.representative_figures_and_works: Carl O. Sauer: “The Morphology of Landscape” (1925); H. C. Darby: Domesday England (1977); W. G. Hoskins: The Making of the English Landscape (1955); J. B. Harley: “Deconstructing the Map” (1989); Doreen Massey: “Places and Their Pasts” (1995); Felix Driver: “Rethinking the Idea of Place” (1995), with Samuel; Raphael Samuel: “Rethinking the Idea of Place” (1995), with Driver; Dolores Hayden: The Power of Place (1995); Paul Carter: The Road to Botany Bay (1987); Ian N. Gregory: “Putting the past in its place” (1998), with Southall; Humphrey Southall: “Putting the past in its place” (1998), with Gregory.

spatialhistory.scope_note: Historical geography has roots well before digital mapping. Spatial history is an overlapping set of approaches, not a synonym for GIS or one unified school. The existing Geography & environmental inquiry entry retains its wider intellectual resources. This selection foregrounds British reconstruction, Australian colonial space and a British HGIS project; wider regional traditions and Indigenous spatial knowledge require fuller treatment. Later digital projects are not backdated into the period reviewed through 2000.

strands.title: Landscape reconstruction and historical traces
strands.focus: Sauer’s morphological programme and Hoskins’s landscape reading offer distinct ways of studying past environments.

strands.title: Reconstructing geography from historical records
strands.focus: Darby works from Domesday evidence; the extent of a source is not identical to the geography of a whole society.

strands.title: Maps as historical representations
strands.focus: Harley asks how power, rhetoric and conventions enter mapmaking. His argument supplies source criticism, not a reason to abandon spatial measurement.

strands.title: Contested places and their pasts
strands.focus: Massey’s relational account appears alongside Driver and Samuel’s spatial-history editorial; co-publication does not imply one shared theory.

strands.title: Colonial naming and spatial narratives
strands.focus: Carter examines Australian territorial representation; this analysis must remain distinct from Indigenous authority over Country.

strands.title: Urban landscapes and public interpretation
strands.focus: Hayden links material places with histories of diverse urban lives.

strands.title: Historical GIS (HGIS) and changing boundaries
strands.focus: Gregory and Southall’s 1998 account links changing administrative units with historical statistics; proposed extensions remain proposals. In Montreal, Olson and her collaborators linked sampled households to streets and lots, with GIS from the 1990s (1997) and in the collective MAP project from 2000.

strands.title: Making Native Space: Colonialism, Resistance, and Reserves in British Columbia
strands.focus: Harris reads competing colonial land policies as spatial arrangements with different consequences for Indigenous lives. Publisher chapter pp. 8–10 only; analysis of Merivale and imperial policy is not Indigenous testimony or an exhaustive account of Indigenous territorial knowledge.
strands.works: Making Native Space: Colonialism, Resistance, and Reserves in British Columbia

strands.title: Demonic Grounds: Black Women and the Cartographies of Struggle
strands.focus: McKittrick treats racial and sexual domination as spatial processes while preserving Black women’s geographic knowledge and contestation. McKittrick explicitly develops a geographic reading of Sylvia Wynter’s critique of the overrepresentation of Man. Chapter 5 pp. 121–123 only, read in the authorized 2020 reprint. Not a new 2020 programme or a whole-book reading. Chapter 5 pp. 122–123; bounded account of her stated use of Wynter. No generalized genealogy or claim of first reception.
strands.works: Demonic Grounds: Black Women and the Cartographies of Struggle

strands.title: Historical GIS: structuring, mapping and analysing geographies of the past
strands.focus: Gregory and Healey describe historical GIS as extending from quantitative into qualitative inquiry and across disciplinary boundaries. Author abstract only; GIS is one method within historical geography, not its beginning or its synonym.
strands.works: Historical GIS: structuring, mapping and analysing geographies of the past

strands.title: Exemplos brasileiros de geografia histórica: considerações sobre as obras de Maurício Abreu e Antonio Carlos Robert Moraes
strands.focus: Machado and Gomes distinguish Abreu’s urban-historical work from Moraes’s inquiries into geopolitics and territorial management in Brazilian historical geography. Portuguese abstract read; English research paraphrase. Their two examples do not exhaust Brazilian scholarship or establish unique founders.
strands.works: Exemplos brasileiros de geografia histórica: considerações sobre as obras de Maurício Abreu e Antonio Carlos Robert Moraes

strands.title: Historical Geography in Brazil: Examining Backgrounds and New Perspectives
strands.focus: Gomes da Silveira calls for historical geography to include Brazilian and other southern sites of knowledge production beyond an English-speaking canon. Indexed publisher abstract only; named networks and institutional history require body-text review. Regional coverage remains partial.
strands.works: Historical Geography in Brazil: Examining Backgrounds and New Perspectives

strands.title: Historical geographies: Translating times and spaces
strands.focus: Legg and coauthors propose multilingual reviews and reflection on translation to broaden historical geography’s disciplinary conversation. Editorial pp. 5–6; proposed journal practice, not evidence of completed decolonization. All five author credits preserved.
strands.works: Historical geographies: Translating times and spaces

strands.title: Producing space through social practice and power
strands.focus: Lefebvre’s 1974 introduction asks how spaces and their codes are produced and changed through social practices, planning and power. Space participates in these relations rather than merely containing them. This is his theoretical proposal; the excerpt neither supplies a GIS procedure nor establishes a uniform school of spatial historians.
strands.works: La production de l’espace (1974), introduction excerpt pp. 19–27; The Production of Space, trans. Donald Nicholson-Smith (1991, metadata only)
